Our people often say the best lessons aren’t taken within the confines of a classroom. They come with age, with living, and with stories told by strangers over an iced coffee in places far from home.

These are the lessons that change you — in ways you never imagined. They shift your thinking, your values, and the very world around you.

At the Ecole de Management du Groupe ISM 
where I’m pursuing my Master’s in International Management (MBA), I feel privileged to have both, the classroom and the world. It’s like having my cake and then getting more cake. 

Last semester, we studied Emerging Markets and Business Development. I explored how countries use small and medium enterprises to transition from agriculture to manufacturing, even designing a business entry strategy for Brazil.

Today was different. For an hour, we learned about Malaysia’s entrepreneurial landscape and how African managers can build better, as Malaysia did.

Throughout that lesson, I felt broken! Broken by the idea that it might take Sierra Leone a hundred years to accomplish what Malaysia did in twenty.

Malaysia, the world’s third-largest producer of palm oil, wasn’t always this way. Palm oil came through British colonization, the same crop Sierra Leone once led in producing. Like us, Malaysia was colonized by Britain, but also by Portugal and Japan. Yet they moved from agriculture to manufacturing, and now toward a fully digital economy, while we remain in a loop, swinging between two parties, some days hopeful, other days not at all.

In the 1980s, Malaysia launched the Look East Policy, learning from Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. They built trade agreements, exchanges, and practical policies that worked.

Meanwhile, Sierra Leone has had multiple development agendas since 2007, yet for the average citizen, little has changed. We spend time drafting hundred-page documents that few read or understand. The line between what’s achievable and what’s not remains blurred.

Our professor today spoke about leadership — vision matched with the willingness to lead change. Start small, he said: fix electricity, water, schools; build partnerships, innovate, expand.

Malaysia also built a strong SME culture. Over 50% of its economy comes from the service sector many led by young people. Entrepreneurship isn’t just taught; it’s supported. There’s even a dedicated SME bank for loans, grants, and mentorship.

In Sierra Leone, while starting a business is easier today, sustaining one isn’t. This isn’t an individual problem, it’s a policy one. The government and private sector must work together to create an ecosystem that supports youth entrepreneurs with both funding and mentorship.

We can do better. We must do better. My hope is that our next president drafts a 20-page (or less) development plan, one every Sierra Leonean can understand, believe in, and rally behind.

OCBC aims to provide social loans to 10,000 women entrepreneurs across Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Indonesia by 2030 through dedicated programmes targeted at small- and medium-sized enterprises (SME).

The bank is a fifth of its way there. As of June, OCBC claims to have supported over 2,000 women entrepreneurs with total social loan commitments of close to $600 million.

The loans are borne out of the OCBC Women Unlimited Programme, which the bank has rolled out in four markets across the region. OCBC launched the programme in Singapore under the name OCBC Women Entrepreneurs Programme, where women-owned SMEs can secure financing of up to $100,000 within the first two years of incorporation. OCBC has also waived the 1.5% “facility fee” levied on approved loan amounts.

Women entrepreneurs are often “a little bit more cautious at the start”, says Linus Goh, head of global commercial banking at OCBC Bank. This makes them less likely to take up a loan early in their business journeys, he adds at a Sept 17 media briefing.

“Lots of entrepreneurs at the beginning — if things were left to themselves — they raise some capital on their own and will exhaust that capital first before they seek help,” says Goh. “But actually the idea is that you draw on a facility concurrent with your capital, and then you have a credit record that starts to develop early, so that gives you the wherewithal to get started well… The stigma of taking the loan earlier was something that we wanted to remove.”

According to OCBC, loan commitments extended to women-owned SMEs in Singapore grew by more than 20% in the 12 months following the launch of the programme in April 2024. Women-owned SMEs in the food and beverage sector received the highest number of loans, followed by those in the building and construction, and transport and logistics sectors.

Read the new Engine by Starling x EY Malaysia piece on "transaction-led digital banking" this morning. The thesis lands. The case studies don't quite carry it.

Every example is a winner. Starling, Cake by VPBank - Digital Bank, OakNorth, Judo Bank, Superbank, Salt Bank, AMP. Conspicuously absent:

Xinja. Australia's first neobank. Shut December 2020. Modern stack, app-first, well capitalised. Died because it offered 2.25% on deposits with no lending book to match. A GlobalData analyst put it bluntly: any bank paying above-market deposit rates with nothing to deploy them into has a problem. Architecture was not the issue.

Volt. Australia's first online-only bank. Cloud-native, modern core. Shut June 2022 with $113m in deposits after a Series F fell through.

N26. Walked away from 500,000 US customers in January 2022 at a $9bn valuation.

Monzo. Just exited the US in March 2026, twelve weeks after finally getting its EU licence through Ireland. The OCC had rejected its US application back in 2021.

If Gen 4 architecture is the moat, four cloud-native banks shouldn't keep failing on it.

Then there's Starling's own story. The piece doesn't mention that Starling's SME book grew from 87,000 to 330,000 clients in under two years on the back of the UK's Bounce Back Loan Scheme, where it issued £1.57bn of 100% government-guaranteed loans. Lord Agnew called it "a cost-free marketing exercise" in 2022. In May 2025, Starling took a £28.2m provision after voluntarily removing government guarantees on loans where its own fraud checks had been inadequate, plus a £29m FCA fine for "shockingly lax" financial crime controls. Profit fell 26%.

The 9.4% SME share is real. It was also assembled inside a once-in-a-generation policy backdrop and an AML system the regulator found materially deficient. Awkward for a piece selling engineering culture as the moat.
The opening example is also off. An Indian food delivery app extending credit on consumption data is embedded lending, not deposit-led primacy. Two different models, one label.

And the causal chain moves too fast. Good UX, engagement, primacy, cheap deposits, profit. In most markets primacy is still anchored by payroll, mortgage and switching friction. Chime has had scale and engagement for years without either primacy or profitability.

One last thing worth naming: the piece is co-authored by Engine by Starling's CCO, with case studies drawn substantially from Engine by Starling's own customer base. Vendors should make their case. It just reads as a point of view, not neutral analysis.

The argument on cost-to-serve, modularity and segment focus is right. I'd just want it stress-tested against Xinja, Volt, N26 US, Monzo US, and the parts of Starling's own P&L the article quietly left out.

Bank Negara Malaysia - Financial Stability Review October 2025

🔹 Domestic financial markets remained orderly despite global volatility

Despite heightened global volatility, driven by US tariff developments, concerns over global growth and geopolitical tensions, Malaysia’s financial market conditions remained orderly. The Financial Market Stress Index (FMSI) peaked in May but has since moderated, reflecting stabilisation across all asset classes.
The ringgit appreciated by 6.1% against the US dollar between March and September 2025, driven largely by external developments. Malaysia’s favourable economic prospects, ongoing structural reforms and continued engagements with corporates are expected to provide ongoing support for the ringgit.

🔹 Business resilience sustained amid cost pressures

In the first half of 2025, business operations remained resilient, supported by resilient domestic demand and sustained economic activity. However, profitability was constrained by persistent cost pressures, particularly in sectors affected by higher labour and material costs. Despite these challenges, businesses maintained their financial strength. The median interest coverage ratio stood at 6.2 times, while the share of firms-at-risk remained stable at 24.4%.

The credit quality of business loans was sustained, with the impairment ratio unchanged at 3.1%. While a small segment of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) continued to face repayment challenges, signs of financial stress remained contained. The share of SME loans under repayment assistance programmes continued to decline, accounting for 4.1% of total SME loans and just 0.7% of total loans in the banking system and development financial institutions.

Looking ahead, the operating environment is expected to remain challenging in the second half of 2025. Nonetheless, moderating input prices and firms’ ongoing cost management strategies are expected to alleviate some of the pressures. Additionally, strong domestic demand and continued investment activity will remain as key pillars supporting business resilience.

🔹 Household resilience anchored by favourable economic and labour market conditions

While the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged slightly higher to 84.8%, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity remained healthy, underpinned by banks’ prudent lending standards. Key indicators of debt repayment capacity remained sound, with the median debt service ratio (DSR) at 41% for newly approved loans and 33% for outstanding loans.

Overall, the quality of household borrowings remained sound, with the loan impairment ratio unchanged at 1.1%. The share of household loans under repayment assistance programmes continued to decline, reflecting sustained repayment behaviour. Despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures, signs of financial stress among household borrowers remained limited and contained, with no evidence of widespread deterioration in repayment trends.

He opened a letter he had received from the Singapore Land Authority (SLA).

It showed a caveat – a legal document obtained by a potential buyer who wants to exercise an option to buy a property – had been lodged by a credit company against a landed property in Katong he owns with his mother."

Not likely to be an option. 🤔 Does the Straits Times not know that there are many kinds of caveats (which is Latin for beware, as in caveat emptor)?

"Mr Kwek, 49, and his partner, Ms Brenda Chow, were surprised...

Mr Kwek, a freelance violinist, called the credit company and learnt that someone had submitted what was supposed to be his NRIC to obtain a loan."

So the caveat was for the security for the loan. 🙄

"The imposter also submitted a notice of assessment, which may have been forged, stating that he had earned an income of $170,000 in 2025 from two companies registered in his name.

Mr Kwek said he has no links to the companies, one registered in 2023 and the other in 2025.

The credit company told him the identity thief had engaged a law firm to lodge the caveat, and further investigations found that the thief had engaged another law firm to secure from SLA a replacement deed for Mr Kwek’s home."

There are no deeds for registered land. What the identity thief must have applied for is a replacement certificate of title.

"The credit company said the imposter had tried to use the property as collateral to get a $2.9 million loan from the credit company.

“They were just one small step away from getting the $2.9 million loan and I’m very sure they would have run away with that money,” said Mr Kwek."

Indeed, he might have gotten away with it if he had gone straight for registration after getting the replacement certificate of title rather than lodge a caveat. If he had managed to do that, Mr Kwek would have found his home security for the loan extended by the credit company because title registries are authoritative even if the owners never authorised the transaction. One reason why Hong Kong's Land Titles Ordinance, enacted in 2004, has never been brought into operation.

Many title registration systems provide insurance against loss but in Singapore, this is only available if the registry was at fault.

"For now, the caveat has been cancelled and Mr Kwek gets to keep his home."

Easily done for caveats, much harder for registrations. But that's the point of title registration: trade off greater security for the acquirer with lesser security for the owner.

"Checks by The Straits Times revealed that he may not be the only victim." 

Be careful what you wish for. If you think obviously fallible checks in the real world is bad, imagine a blockchain land registry where you are one hack/wrench away from losing your home. 🙄

Reading this update reminded me of a recurring challenge I’ve often seen play out, particularly with SMEs and startups in emerging markets: they are rich in ideas but poor in how those ideas are valued.

Many SMEs actually hold strong IP portfolios with real potential to be monetized. The difficulty, however, is that traditional accounting frameworks rarely recognize these assets. As a result, banks and investors often treat them as invisible, even when they are the true drivers of enterprise value.

This is why the analogy of IP as the dark matter of the global economy deeply resonates. We all know it’s there, shaping outcomes, yet we rarely measure it and even more rarely finance against it.

The WIPO–MIDF pilot in Malaysia is, in my view, a much-needed experiment. I have seen too many African founders whose innovations never scale beyond local markets simply because they could not collateralize their IP. Imagine what becomes possible if this barrier is broken.

But there is also a cultural side to this story that feels equally important. Too often, SMEs treat IP registration as the final goal — a certificate to be framed and displayed. Gone are the days when the narrative should stop at registration. From personal experience, a vast majority of SMEs are now aware of copyright, patents, trademarks, and design rights. What remains largely unknown, however, is how to leverage these rights as collateral for loans and other forms of financing.

As the case of MyB Innovation shows, protection is only the beginning. True value emerges when IP becomes the springboard for commercialization, partnerships, and global scaling. That mindset shift is as critical as any financing pilot.

This is also a clear call to action for policymakers in regions like Africa, where creative industries, agritech, fintech, and medtech are booming. If ASEAN can push the boundaries on IP financing and valuation, there is no reason why Africa cannot take inspiration and adapt similar models to its own realities.

Equally, there is a need for more campaigns and awareness on IP financing, not just IP awareness. The narrative must evolve if we want transformative change for SMEs

Financing Africa’s SMEs through Securitization: Unlocking Capital for Inclusive Growth

This paper examines the potential role of securitization in addressing the persistent financing gap confronting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Africa. 

Despite SMEs accounting for a substantial share of firms, employment and productive activity across the continent, access to finance remains constrained by structural weaknesses including collateral limitations, information asymmetries, shallow capital markets and weak financial intermediation systems. 

The paper argues that the financing challenge facing African SMEs extends beyond conventional credit shortages and increasingly reflects broader deficiencies in market design and liquidity allocation. 

Securitization, defined as the transformation of illiquid financial assets and future cash flows into tradable securities, is explored as an innovative financing mechanism capable of mobilising broader pools of domestic and international capital. 

The paper examines key channels through which securitization can support SME financing, including receivables securitization, trade finance securitization and future revenue stream securitization. 

Drawing on recent international experiences involving multilateral development institutions and emerging structured finance initiatives, the paper highlights both opportunities and regulatory considerations associated with implementation. 

It concludes that while securitization offers important prospects for expanding SME access to finance and strengthening capital market development, its effectiveness ultimately depends on robust regulatory frameworks, institutional readiness and market credibility.

It needs fintech that earns trust at the barangay level.
The future is about financial behaviors, not just digital accounts.

The real winners?
Those who combine credit, commerce, community — and confidence.

In United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd v Tan Chong Whatt & Anor, the Court of Appeal delivered a significant judgment in 2024 on the personal liability of directors who sign bank guarantees as principal debtors, meaning they are treated as if they personally took the loan rather than merely backing someone else's obligation.

The company had been wound up. The directors, who had signed the bank facility agreement as both guarantors and as principal debtors, assumed that the winding up order capped their personal exposure. Section 8(2A) of the Insolvency Act 1967 limits the interest that can be claimed against the company after a winding up order. The directors relied on this as protection against post-winding up interest claims.

The Court of Appeal rejected this position. Section 8(2A) applies to the debtor, meaning the company that has been wound up. A director who has additionally signed as a principal debtor is not a mere surety, meaning not simply a backup payer who steps in only if the company defaults. They have contractually assumed primary liability as if they personally borrowed the money. The statutory cap protecting the company does not extend to them. Their liability for post-winding up interest continues to accumulate until the debt is fully discharged.

The court's reasoning followed the Federal Court in Andrew Lee Siew Ling v United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, which had established that guarantors who agree to be principal debtors cannot rely on the surety protection provisions in Sections 92 and 94 of the Contracts Act 1950, because they have taken on more than a surety's role.

Most Malaysian bank facility agreements for SME borrowers include a guarantee and indemnity document containing both a guarantee clause and a principal debtor clause. Directors who sign both without understanding the distinction are assuming personal liability that survives the company's winding up and is not subject to the statutory interest cap.

The structural protections that are available but rarely negotiated include a capped guarantee limiting personal exposure to a specific ringgit amount, a specific facility guarantee limiting scope to a named facility rather than all present and future debts under an all-monies clause, and a release mechanism defining the conditions under which the guarantee is discharged.

None of these protections are automatic. They must be specifically negotiated before signing. Banks will not always agree. But the conversation must happen before the guarantee is signed, not after the company is wound up and the interest continues to run.

Think about the most recent personal guarantee you or someone in your network signed for a company bank facility. Was the principal debtor clause specifically explained before signing? YES or NO in the comments. I read every reply.

Malaysia Cannot Build High Wages on Low Productivity MSMEs

• Malaysia’s MSMEs Are Stuck in Survival Mode

• Why Malaysia’s MSMEs Struggle to Create Real Wealth

The OECD’s 2026 SME Scoreboard, which includes Malaysia in a 48 country comparison and a dedicated country snapshot, shows a financing environment that is still tight, expensive, and biased toward survival rather than investment (p. 5, p. 10, p. 143 to 144).  

The numbers are hard to ignore. Across the scoreboard, 34 out of 39 countries still had SME borrowing costs above pre pandemic levels, 10 out of 17 countries showed a higher share of SMEs requiring collateral, and new SME lending only recovered 5.7% in 2024 after a 9% decline in 2023. Even then, lending was still 4% below 2022, while long term SME loans edged down again (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).  

That is the pressure point for Malaysia. When credit is expensive and short dated, MSMEs stay trapped in working capital mode. They delay equipment upgrades, digitisation, expansion, and the hiring of stronger talent. Inference: that is how stagnant wages become structural, not cyclical, because firms are financing survival instead of capability building. The report does not measure Malaysian wages directly, but it clearly shows the financing pattern that keeps wage growth weak (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).  

The rest of the data points in the same direction. Factoring fell 3% in 2024 and leasing rose only 1.6%, so alternative finance is still too shallow to change the capital base of small firms. Venture capital recovered in 18 out of 30 countries, but the rebound was uneven and concentrated in a few large artificial intelligence deals. At the same time, fintech driven finance and non bank lenders are becoming more important, which means the market is changing, but not yet enough to solve the core constraint (p. 18 to 19).  

The solution is not more credit in name. It is better credit architecture. The OECD points to asset based finance, leasing, factoring, government guarantees, direct lending, digital invoice registries, and AI enabled underwriting as practical tools to widen access and move firms from survival credit to investment credit. It also calls for better data on loan stock and flow, collateral, fees, gender ownership, and geography, because weak measurement leads to weak policy (p. 14 to 16, p. 18 to 19, p. 27 to 28).  

For Malaysia, If MSMEs remain undercapitalised, productivity will stay weak, wages will stay sticky, and talent will keep flowing toward firms or countries that can pay for capability. The real reform target is not more rhetoric around SME support. It is a shift from survival credit to investment credit, and from low productivity competition to high productivity competition (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).

COP 30 Belém - The COP of Implementation, Not Intention

With COP 30 begins today in Belém, Brazil, global attention turns to how this COP will shift from pledges to delivery.

At the Climate Governance Malaysia Global Summit 2025, we heard directly from Bruna Cerqueira - Action Agenda Coordinator for the COP 30 Presidency; her message was clear: this COP will be collectively built, “in the spirit of Mutirão” (Brazilian for working together).

What to Expect from COP Belém
📌 Implementation first: Six axes: Energy, Nature, Agriculture, Cities, Social Development anchored by finance + technology + capacity building.

📌 Stable frameworks: ~400 existing initiatives consolidated into 30 objectives, forming activation groups for collective delivery.

📌 Finance as enabler: A new Finance Ministers’ Circle aims to turn the USD 1.3 trillion finance roadmap into real investment flows through de-risking and blended finance.

📌 Nature and equity at the centre: Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Fund (TFFF) rewards forest stewardship, restoration, and indigenous participation through an investment-based model.

📌 From rules to real impact: Policies must connect to communities and SMEs-the people’s COP in practice.

My Reflection - Through a Banker’s Lens

What resonates most is the pivot from policy to practicality.

This COP invites financiers, corporates and regulators to turn intent into bankable pathways.

1️⃣ Implementation generates implementation.
Pilot → prove → scale. Banks must design risk-sharing structures that attract first movers; once projects prove cashflow, mainstream capital follows.

2️⃣Adaptation is credit protection.
Climate resilience isn’t philanthropy: it protects repayment capacity. Embedding climate scenarios into risk and pricing models will future-proof portfolios, especially for SME supply chains.

3️⃣ Nature as a financial asset class.
Nature-based solutions can underwrite performance-linked loans and guarantees. Frameworks like CCPT already guide Malaysian bankers, hence the next step is to translate biodiversity services into economic value with credible MRV (Measurement-Reporting-Verification) models.

4️⃣ South-South innovation and learning.
Brazil’s revolving fund model and community custodianship mirror Malaysia’s inclusive transition finance goals. Blending public capital, DFIs and local bank expertise can unlock scale.

5️⃣ Bring the “blockers.”
Bruna was clear: don’t come only with aspirations, come with solutions. Let’s table real bottlenecks - data gaps, permits, FX risk, PPA bankability, so COP can help shape enabling conditions.

As COP Belém begins, let’s move from commitments to capital flow.

My experience:
In 2021-2022, during my MBA at The Banking and Finance Academy of the Republic of Uzbekistan, I dedicated my dissertation to exploring loan products that align with the principles of Islamic Finance. My focus was on Musharaka and its widely practiced variation, Musharaka al-Mutanaqisa. These models offer ethical, partnership-based alternatives to conventional lending, with strong potential for implementation in developing financial markets.

To further deepen my knowledge in this field, from September to December 2024, I completed a professional qualification course on AAOIFI Shariah Standards at the Banking and Finance Academy of the Republic of Uzbekistan. This experience gave me a solid foundation in the internationally recognized framework of Islamic finance governance, and I had the opportunity to engage with expert instructors and peers who are equally passionate about Shariah-compliant financial innovation.

How it works:
Musharaka is a joint venture structure where two or more parties invest capital and share profits and losses based on agreed terms and Shariah Standarts in priority.
Musharaka al-Mutanaqisa allows one partner (the client) to gradually purchase the bank’s share in an asset, ultimately becoming the sole owner. This model is especially suitable for real estate, home financing, and SME development.

Globally, Musharaka-based financing has been adopted in countries such as the UK, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE—providing Sharia-compliant solutions in housing, infrastructure, and business financing.

Uzbekistan now stands at a key moment for Islamic Finance development. With increasing public interest, supportive regulatory movements, and an ideal geographic location, the country is well-positioned to introduce and scale products based on Islamic financial principles. Musharaka al-Mutanaqisa, in particular, holds promise for ethical home financing and inclusive SME growth.

With this academic background and hands-on exposure, I am more committed than ever to supporting the development of Islamic Finance in Uzbekistan and contributing to meaningful, values-driven financial solutions.

In addition to #employment income, many Malaysians today earn supplementary income through freelancing, consulting, or online businesses. Such income, regardless of scale, remains taxable and must be declared accurately. Failure to do so may expose taxpayers to penalties during audits.

Understanding #Rental Income and  #Allowable Deductions
Rental income is another area that requires careful attention. While rental earnings are fully taxable, taxpayers are entitled to claim specific deductions such as loan interest, assessment and quit rent, insurance, and routine repairs and maintenance. However, it is important to distinguish between revenue and capital expenses. #Renovations, extensions, and property improvements are considered capital in nature and are not deductible.

#New Dividend Tax Rules for YA 2025
An important development for YA 2025 is the introduction of a 2% tax on dividend income exceeding RM100,000 received by individuals. While dividends under Malaysia’s single-tier system remain generally tax-exempt, this threshold introduces a new layer of consideration in personal tax planning. It signals increased scrutiny on higher-income taxpayers and highlights the importance of a more strategic approach to dividend income. Taxpayers should assess the total amount of dividends received annually.

🕌 Islamic Finance Series — Financing with Compassion and Integrity. 🤝🌍

🟢 In today’s profit-driven world, the concept of interest-free lending feels almost impossible — yet Islamic finance has preserved it for centuries under one timeless principle: Qard Hasan (قرض حسن) — the benevolent loan.

It’s not about profit.
It’s about purpose.
It’s where finance meets faith, and money becomes a means of mercy. 🌙✨

🌿 1️⃣ What Is Qard Hasan? — “A Loan for the Sake of Allah”

💡 Principle:
A Qard Hasan is an interest-free loan extended out of goodwill to help someone in need or to support ethical, productive ventures.
The borrower is required to repay only the principal, with no additional return — and any voluntary gesture (without prior condition) is considered a reward, not riba.

✅ How It Works:
1️⃣ The lender provides funds to support personal or business needs.
2️⃣ The borrower repays the same amount after a defined period.
3️⃣ No interest, no exploitation, no uncertainty.
4️⃣ If the borrower faces hardship, repayment can be extended or forgiven.

⚙️ Example:
🔹 A small entrepreneur receives $10,000 as a Qard Hasan to start a tailoring business.
🔹 After one year, she repays $10,000.
🔹 If she adds $500 voluntarily in gratitude, it’s an act of goodwill — not an obligation.

💼 2️⃣ Applications of Qard Hasan in Modern Finance
Qard Hasan is not limited to charity — it’s an empowerment tool used by Islamic banks, governments, and NGOs for financial inclusion and community development.

💠 Used For:
🔹 Microfinance and SME empowerment
🔹 Student and education funding
🔹 Emergency and social welfare loans
🔹 Support for startups and ethical entrepreneurship

💠 Institutional Examples:
🏦 Islamic banks like Al Baraka, Meezan, and Bank Islam offer Qard Hasan-based microloans.
💡 Zakat and Waqf institutions use it to empower underprivileged individuals to become self-reliant.

⚖️ 3️⃣ Qard Hasan vs Conventional Loan

🟠 Conventional Loan: -	Profit generation,	Interest (Riba), Commercial, Rigid repayment, 	Debt burden

🟢 Islamic Qard Hasan: Social & ethical support, 	Principal only, Benevolence (Ihsan), Can defer or forgive, 	Empowerment

🌙 4️⃣ Qard Hasan in Trade & Development
Qard Hasan isn’t charity — it’s productive compassion.
When embedded in trade finance, it supports:
🔹 Producers during cash flow shortages
🔹 Farmers between harvest cycles
🔹 Exporters facing shipment delays
🔹 Women entrepreneurs and youth ventures

It builds an economy where trust replaces interest, and mutual uplift replaces exploitation.

🌍 5️⃣ Global Impact
Countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Sudan have integrated Qard Hasan into microfinance ecosystems — helping thousands rise from debt to dignity.

💠 Emerging Trends:
🔹 Qard Hasan crowdfunding platforms

🔹 KLIBOR is Being Phased Out — Introducing MYOR & MYOR-i

A closer look at Malaysia’s new transaction-based benchmarks 👇

💡 Malaysia to Retire KLIBOR by 2029 — Transition to MYOR and MYOR-i

Bank Negara Malaysia will phase out KLIBOR (Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate) by January 1, 2029, replacing it with MYOR (Malaysia Overnight Rate) and MYOR-i — transaction-based benchmarks reflecting actual overnight interbank trades.

📘 What They Are
	•	KLIBOR: Historically, the reference rate banks used to lend to each other and price loans, bonds, and derivatives. It was based on estimates submitted by selected banks, even if no trades occurred.
	•	MYOR: Calculated from actual overnight interbank lending transactions, making the rate more accurate, transparent, and reliable for conventional banking products.
	•	MYOR-i: The Islamic finance equivalent of MYOR. It reflects actual Shariah-compliant overnight interbank transactions, providing a benchmark for Islamic loans, sukuk, and financing products while adhering to Shariah principles.

Why this matters:
	1.	Accuracy & Reliability – reflects real market activity, harder to manipulate.
	2.	Transparency – verifiable by market participants and regulators.
	3.	Risk Management – helps banks and businesses predict borrowing costs.
	4.	Global Alignment – consistent with international benchmarks like SOFR (US) and SONIA (UK).

Analogy:
	•	KLIBOR = “I think I can lend at 3.5% today.” (estimate)
	•	MYOR = “Banks actually lent at 3.45% today.” (fact-based)
	•	MYOR-i = “Islamic banks actually lent at 3.45% via Shariah-compliant methods today.” (fact-based, Shariah-compliant)

💥 Who Will Be Impacted

🏦 Banks & Financial Institutions – corporate, SME, and institutional clients with KLIBOR-linked loans, bonds, and derivatives need updated pricing models, systems, and contracts.
🏢 Corporates & SMEs – review financing agreements and fallback clauses.
💰 Islamic Banks – migrate to MYOR-i for Shariah-compliant products.
📊 Investors & Fund Managers – adjust valuations for sukuk, bonds, and derivatives.

👥 Retail Customers – not directly affected, as personal loans use Base Rate (BR) or Base Lending Rate (BLR), but benefit indirectly from a more stable, transparent financial system.

This transition is more than a rate change — it’s part of modernizing Malaysia’s financial infrastructure for a transparent, data-driven, and globally aligned future.

Access to credit can help MSMEs expand operations, manage seasonal demand, and stabilise cash flow. However, the true cost of borrowing extends far beyond the advertised interest rate and EMI. Many additional charges and structural terms quietly increase the effective repayment burden. Understanding these factors is essential to protecting working capital, profitability, and long-term creditworthiness.

Here are the 8 Hidden Costs MSMEs Often Overlook:

• Processing fees and upfront deductions that reduce the actual capital received
 • Documentation, legal, valuation, and collateral-related expenses
 • Prepayment and foreclosure charges, including lock-in clauses
 • Penal interest, late payment fees, and EMI bounce charges
 • Bundled insurance and optional add-ons added to the principal
 • GST at 18% on service-related loan charges
 • Flat-rate interest structures that increase effective repayment
 • Opportunity cost of over-borrowing and paying interest on unused capital

Hidden costs do not necessarily imply unfair practices. Most are disclosed in loan documents. The real challenge arises when these terms are not examined closely before signing. To ensure smarter and safer borrowing, MSMEs must: 

• Review the sanction letter thoroughly before acceptance
• Request a complete written breakup of all fees and taxes
• Compare total repayment amount, not just the EMI
• Examine whether the loan follows a flat or reducing balance method
• Assess prepayment flexibility and foreclosure conditions
• Align EMI schedules with business cash flow cycles
• Maintain a repayment buffer to avoid penalties
• Borrow strictly based on actual business requirements
• Monitor the business credit profile periodically
• Choose RBI-regulated institutions that follow transparent lending practices

Responsible borrowing is not about avoiding credit. It is about understanding the full cost before committing. When evaluated carefully, credit becomes a strategic growth tool rather than a financial burden.

📊 Malaysia’s credit cycle: What the latest trend is really signalling

Loan growth started the year strongly in Q1, but forward-looking indicators now point to a gradual easing of momentum in the months ahead. While this may look like a simple slowdown in lending, I see it reflecting a broader, healthier shift in borrowing behaviour.

🧠 Understanding the signal
Moderating credit growth isn’t just a banking metric—it mirrors economic behaviour, risk appetite, and confidence. Typically, it suggests:

· More selective business expansion
· Greater focus on cash flow and balance sheet strength
· Reduced reliance on leverage
· More disciplined risk-taking among corporates and SMEs

This phase doesn’t automatically mean economic weakness. It often marks a mid-cycle normalisation, especially after periods of stronger growth and tighter financial conditions.

🌏 Malaysia in the ASEAN context
Credit cycles vary across the region:
🇲🇾 Malaysia – moderate growth with early signs of cooling; a shift toward quality-focused lending
🇮🇩 Indonesia – still expanding, supported by domestic consumption
🇻🇳 Vietnam – higher growth but more cyclical
🇸🇬 Singapore – structurally stable, less credit-driven
🇹🇭 Thailand – slower credit growth amid softer domestic demand

Malaysia appears to be transitioning earlier than some peers into a more balanced, disciplined phase.

🏦 How banks typically respond
In this environment, banks tend to:

· Gradually tighten underwriting standards
· Prioritise asset quality over loan volume
· Build stronger credit risk buffers
· Favour sustainable borrowers over aggressive expansion

These are standard adjustments that support long-term stability.

📉 What it means for the economy, businesses & consumers
Economy: slower expansion but more efficient capital allocation, reduced overheating risks.
Businesses: more selective financing access, advantage for strong cash-flow companies, phased expansion plans.
Consumers: cautious borrowing, stricter loan approvals, slower household debt growth—but gradual improvement in financial resilience.

⚖️ Final take: where Malaysia is heading
We’re not in a credit boom, nor entering a contraction. The direction is best described as a gradual transition toward a more disciplined, quality-focused credit environment. It’s a mid-cycle normalisation where credit continues to grow, but with fewer excesses and stronger risk controls. The trajectory points to stability with moderation—healthier long-term conditions, even if momentum feels slower compared to peak cycles.

Over the past couple of years, we have seen a very noticeable shift in the SME lending world.

Lenders are no longer simply relying on statutory accounts that may already be 9–18 months old by the time they are reviewed. Increasingly, they want to understand what is happening in a business today.

Current management information (MI) is becoming a far more important part of the underwriting and credit review process for SMEs.

When we talk about management accounts or management information, this can include items such as:

• Monthly or quarterly profit & loss statements
• Balance sheets
• Cash flow reports and forecasts
• Bank statements
• VAT returns
• Sales trends and pipeline activity
• Aged debtors and creditors
• Commentary around trading performance and current business conditions

Many SMEs are not always best served by relying solely on year end external accounting support. Having some level of ongoing financial oversight, management accounting support, or outsourced finance assistance can make a significant difference, not only in helping business owners better manage performance, but also in strengthening a funding case.

Good quality MI can help demonstrate current trading strength, cash flow position, and importantly, a business’s ability to comfortably service debt. In many cases, it is the recent improved business story and current trading performance that helps get a deal over the line.

One thing that still surprises me, however, is how difficult it can sometimes be for businesses to quickly provide this type of information when requested by lenders. Delays in producing MI, incomplete information, or simply not having visibility on the numbers can slow deals down considerably and sometimes kill opportunities altogether.

At Pathway Commercial Finance, we are seeing lenders place increasing emphasis on visibility, cash flow management, and current affordability when assessing SME funding proposals.

Strong MI shows organisation, control, and direction. If a business is improving, growing, or stabilising, it is far better to be prepared and able to clearly demonstrate that story upfront.

CGTMSE – A Pain or a Gain?

Many entrepreneurs consider CGTMSE the best funding option because it is collateral-free.

But is "unsecured" always the best choice?

CGTMSE was created to support deserving MSMEs, especially first-generation entrepreneurs, manufacturers, and growing businesses that have strong potential but lack sufficient collateral to obtain bank finance.

It is an excellent scheme when used for its intended purpose.

However, today many borrowers opt for CGTMSE simply to avoid offering collateral, even when they possess adequate security. Before making that decision, it is important to understand the actual cost.

What Most Borrowers Overlook
✅ Higher interest rates compared to secured loans
✅ Initial CGTMSE guarantee fees in addition to bank processing charges
✅ Annual guarantee service fees throughout the loan tenure
✅ Higher overall cost of borrowing over the long term

In many cases, CGTMSE-backed facilities may also offer less flexibility when it comes to temporary overdrafts, ad-hoc limits, or special credit accommodations compared to well-secured accounts.

The Right Question

Don't ask:
"Can I get a CGTMSE loan?"

Ask:
"Is CGTMSE the right funding structure for my business?"

If you genuinely lack collateral, CGTMSE can be a game-changing opportunity.

But if quality collateral is available, a secured facility may provide lower interest costs, better banking flexibility, and stronger long-term funding support.

Final Thought
CGTMSE is neither a pain nor a gain by itself.

It is simply a financial tool.

The key is choosing the funding product that best supports your business growth—not just the one that avoids collateral.

Smart entrepreneurs compare the total cost of funds, not just the security requirement.

How SME Loans Quietly Deteriorate Before Becoming “Non-Performing” (Malaysia Context)

SME loan defaults rarely happen overnight.
In most cases, observable liquidity deterioration begins 3–6 months prior to missed instalments
The signals are often behavioural and working capital driven rather than headline profitability declines.

1)  Overdraft is persistently maxed out. 💣 
- OD utilization is constantly > 90%. 
- Repeated excess beyond temporary seasonality. 
- Frequent limit breaches. 
> This signals a cash deficit and becomes a permanent funding rather than a cushion or bridge for cash flow. 

2) Deterioration in Cash Conversion Cycle. 💸 
- Debtor days (DSO) extending without revenue growth. 
- Inventory days (DIO) increasing despite flat sales. 
- Creditor days (DPO) stretching beyond historical norms.
> This signals a possible liquidity stress in balance sheet movements before it manifests in P&L erosion. 

3) Maturity mismatch in facility utilisation. ❌ 
- Short term facilities used to fund CAPEX.
- Continuous and persistent rollover of trade lines. 
- Increasing reliance on ad-hoc temporary facilities.
> This introduces a duration mismatch risk of which will further stress out liquidity.

4) Behavioral shifts.😨 
- Delayed submission of financial information.
- Sudden requests for extension or temporary relief.
- Avoidance of discussions are often early indicators of financial strain.
> Behavorial shifts often precede financial disclosure deterioration. 

Early identification enables proactive intervention by facility resizing, collateral enhancement, or restructuring before the occurrence of full impairment. By the time the first instalment is missed, the deterioration has typically been compounding beneath the surface.

(Valuation) Boss, RM5 Million Sales Does Not Mean Your Company Is Worth RM5 Million

Last week, I asked one SME boss a simple question.
“Boss, how much do you think your company is worth?”

He answered very confidently.

“Mr Koh, last year sales RM5 million. So company value should be around RM5million lah.”

I smiled. This is where many SME bosses get valuation wrong.

Sales RM5million does not mean company value RM5 million.

A buyer does not pay you because your sales look big.
A buyer pays for profit.
A buyer pays for cash flow.
A buyer pays for systems.
A buyer pays for customers that can stay.
A buyer pays for a business that can still run after the boss walks out.

This is the painful part.

To the boss, the company is his baby.
30 years of hard work.
Sunday also work.
Public holiday also answer customer call.
Bank loan, supplier pressure, staff problem, customer problem, IRB letter, everything also he handles.

So when someone says the company may not be worth what he thinks, he feels hurt.

But valuation is not based on feeling.

A company with RM5 million sales but only 2% net margin may be less attractive than a smaller company with RM3 million sales and strong recurring profit.

Revenue is nice for storytelling.
Profit is nicer for valuation.
Cash flow is even nicer.
And clean documentation is the most beautiful.

Many SME bosses also think audited accounts already equal valuation.
No.
Audited accounts answer one question : “Are the financial statements fairly presented?”

Valuation asks another question : “What will a serious buyer actually pay for this business?”

Very different question.
Because a buyer will ask:

Are the profits sustainable?
Are customers too dependent on the founder?
Are personal expenses mixed inside the company?
Are directors’ salaries at market rate?
Are related party transactions properly recorded?
Can the business continue without the boss sitting in office every day?

If the answer is no, the value will be discounted.
Sometimes very heavily.

Now valuation is no longer only for selling business.
It matters for Capital Gains Tax on unlisted shares.
It matters for stamp duty on share transfers.
It matters for succession planning.
It matters when shareholders want to exit.
It matters when family business passes to the next generation.
It matters when IRB asks, “How did you arrive at this value?”

The biggest mistake?

Many SME owners only think about valuation when someone wants to buy their company.

By then, too late already.

Value is built years before the sale.
Clean accounts.
Less boss dependency.
Better margins.
Good systems.
Clear documents.
Proper governance.

All these boring things make buyers pay better.

So boss, don’t wait until someone offers you a low price, then only get angry and say : “Why my business so cheap?”

PS : Authored by Mr Koh Teck Peng, Chartered Accountant, Malaysia and Member of IACV (International Association of Certified Valuators).

Navigating Thailand’s Economic Crossroads Amid U.S. Reciprocal Tariffs.

The recent implementation of Reciprocal Tariffs by the United States, aimed at ensuring trade parity, has placed Thailand under a 19% tariff rate — comparable to Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Cambodia, while Vietnam faces a slightly higher rate of 20%. Unlike traditional tariffs designed primarily for revenue generation, this measure serves as a strategic negotiation tool to press trading partners toward fairer market access.

Attending the seminar “Trump Tariffs: Thailand’s Economic Crossroads Post-Negotiation” provided valuable insights into the geopolitical and economic dynamics shaping global trade. From this perspective, Thailand’s response to this shifting trade environment requires a systematic, three-phase approach:

𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Mitigation and Economic Stabilization
The immediate priority should be mitigating the shock from global trade disruptions. Businesses must optimize production and supply chains, leveraging technology to cut costs. At the same time, the government should support vulnerable sectors through targeted tax measures, low-interest loans for SMEs, tax incentives to sustain employment, and strategic efforts to attract foreign direct investment (FDI) — an area where Thailand’s comparatively moderate tariff rate could serve as a competitive advantage.

𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘂𝗺-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Structural Adjustment and Capacity Building
To reduce vulnerability, Thailand must diversify its economy and strengthen its global competitiveness. This includes expanding export reach to high-growth regions such as South Asia, Africa, and Middle East, while supporting SMEs with financial liquidity, market entry facilitation, and platforms for reskilling and upskilling workers in digital and high-tech industries. These steps would build a more resilient economic base capable of withstanding future disruptions.

𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Innovation-Driven Transformation
Thailand must evolve from a contract-driven manufacturer to an innovation-driven economy capable of setting trends and standards in global markets. This transformation will require significant investment in education and workforce development in fields such as AI, STEM, and advanced manufacturing, alongside increased funding for R&D collaborations between the private sector and academia. Furthermore, aligning with global environmental and sustainability standards — including carbon reduction, renewable energy adoption, and supply-chain traceability — will be critical for maintaining market access and global credibility.

By pursuing this three-phase strategy, Thailand can move beyond merely weathering the current trade turbulence to laying a resilient, innovation-driven foundation for long-term growth and competitiveness.

Same drawdown. Very different cost.

We recently worked with a client who was looking at drawing down £9,000 over 3 months, and we compared the cost of using Capital on Tap against a Flexible Line of Credit.

The difference was significant.

With Capital on Tap, the interest came out at £1,308.
With a Flexible Line of Credit, the same amount over the same term came out at £629.

That is less than half the cost.

When does a borrower's past stop defining their future?

The conversation around credit history in Nigeria often centres on the consequences of default. But what we rarely discuss at the policy level is the pathway back.

A credit bureau system that only records failure without providing structured rehabilitation does two things: it creates a permanent underclass of excluded enterprises, and it reduces the total pool of bankable businesses in an economy that desperately needs growth.

Here's what concerns me most.

The current system assumes that time alone heals credit wounds. But SMEs operating in our macroeconomic environment face shocks that are often systemic — forex volatility, input cost inflation, or supply chain disruptions that have nothing to do with management competence.

Yet their credit records treat all defaults as equal moral failures.

Progressive credit history frameworks in other markets include provisions for: graduated rehabilitation timelines based on debt clearance milestones, distinctions between economic-driven and willful defaults, and formal mechanisms for rebuilding creditworthiness through supervised lending windows.

We need these conversations at the regulatory table.

The Central Bank's guidelines on credit reporting are comprehensive on capture and retention. But they're almost silent on restoration and reintegration.

This isn't just about fairness. It's about economic efficiency.

Every viable business locked out of formal finance either migrates to predatory informal channels or shuts down entirely. Both outcomes shrink our tax base, reduce employment, and weaken the financial system's reach.

If we're serious about deepening financial inclusion and supporting Nigeria's real economy, we need credit systems that are designed for resilience, not just compliance.

Common Question: What will business finance cost?

What’s the interest rate?
Rates vary depending on:

• Security available
• Term length
• Type of facility

But the headline rate alone doesn’t tell you the full story.

Are there arrangement or early repayment fees?
Some facilities include:
• Arrangement fees
• Documentation fees
• Early settlement charges

Others build costs into the structure.

Understanding fee mechanics is critical to comparing options accurately.

Is it fixed or variable?
• Fixed rates give certainty and predictable repayments.
• Variable rates may track base rate movements and offer flexibility.
The right choice depends on your appetite for risk and market conditions.

What’s the total repayable amount?
This is the number that matters.
Look at:
• Total cost of capital
• Monthly impact on cashflow
• Return generated from using the funds

The key question is:
“Will this generate a return greater than the cost?”

Chinese SMEs expand into ASEAN through digital-first model

Chinese small and medium enterprises (SME) are accelerating expansion into Southeast Asia through low-cost digital strategies as war and shifting supply chains push firms to diversify beyond their home market, according to OCBC Bank (Hong Kong) Ltd.

OCBC is positioning its Hong Kong and Singapore network to capture rising cross-border activity as mainland Chinese and Hong Kong firms expand into ASEAN markets including Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia.

“The key trend is they will build brands targeting overseas middle-class customers and leverage e-commerce platforms for quicker market entry,” Mimi Tsang, head of commercial banking cash, emerging business at OCBC Bank, told Asian Banking & Finance.

Consumer goods, digital solutions, logistics and environmental, social and governance-related businesses are among the sectors driving outbound expansion, she added.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in April rolled out measures identifying “quality” SMEs and encouraged local governments to support overseas expansion through financing, tax, and industrial policies, according to state-owned news agency Xinhua.

“We see our clients using Hong Kong for capital structuring and treasuries, whilst Singapore serves as their ASEAN operation hub,” Tsang said via Zoom.

She said firms continue to face financing, compliance, and operational challenges even with digital-first expansion models. One issue that SMEs often face when expanding overseas is lack of financing, she pointed out.

OCBC’s regional network spans 250 branches across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam, giving SMEs local banking access without rebuilding relationships in each market.

Tsang said SMEs are also increasingly seeking support beyond financing, including tax, legal, and compliance guidance as they navigate unfamiliar regulatory environments and fragmented supply chains.

The rapid growth in young populations and the middle class will also push SMEs to go global, Tsang said.

OCBC earlier revealed plans to more than double its support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) through sustainable financing.

The Singapore-headquartered bank aims to support 12,000 SMEs across Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Indonesia by 2028, up from just 5,000 in 2025, it said in an April announcement.

Commitments will include social loans as well as dedicated programmes to women entrepreneurs and women-led businesses in the four markets.

OCBC expects this move to drive its SME sustainable finance commitments from nearly $10.14b (S$13b) to $19.5b (S$25b) by 2028.

Sectors that drove the growth included building and construction, manufacturing, and transport and logistics.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

→ Working capital assessment

✔ Cash flow forecasts
✔ Projected balance sheet
✔ Assumption-based growth models

DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio)

Banks want confidence that the business generates enough income to repay debt comfortably.

❌ Low DSCR = high rejection risk
✔ Strong DSCR = stronger approval probability

Many business owners spend decades building wealth…
but very few spend enough time planning how to protect it for their families.

The reality is — business comes with risk.

Over the past few years alone, we have seen:
• COVID-19 disrupt entire industries
• Rising interest rates and inflation
• Supply chain challenges
• Global geopolitical tensions including the Iran-Israel conflict
• Economic uncertainty affecting SMEs and cash flow worldwide

Even strong and established businesses can face unexpected financial pressure.

According to Malaysia’s Insolvency Department and related reports:
• Malaysia recorded thousands of bankruptcy cases annually post-pandemic
• Individuals aged 35–44 formed the largest bankruptcy group between 2020–2024 (Sinar Daily)
• Business loans remain among the major contributors to insolvency cases (Sinar Daily)
• Over 5,000 youths below age 34 were declared bankrupt from 2020 onwards (The Star)

This is why proper wealth structuring, succession planning and asset protection matter.

Living trusts and properly structured policy arrangements may help families create clearer separation and continuity planning — particularly when done early, transparently and in good faith.

As highlighted in legal and insolvency discussions:
✔ timing matters
✔ intent matters
✔ proper documentation matters

Structures created genuinely for succession, family protection and long-term planning are very different from last-minute arrangements intended to avoid creditors.

Many business owners focus heavily on:
✔ growing assets
✔ expanding businesses
✔ increasing revenue

…but neglect:
❌ estate planning
❌ liquidity planning
❌ succession arrangements
❌ family financial continuity

The question is not whether risk exists.
The question is whether your family is prepared if something unexpected happens.

We cannot predict the future — but we can prepare for it wisely.

If you are a business owner, entrepreneur or professional, this is a conversation worth having early, not during a crisis.

Legacy Advisor.

(Valuation) Boss, RM5 Million Sales Does Not Mean Your Company Is Worth RM5 Million

Last week, I asked one SME boss a simple question.
“Boss, how much do you think your company is worth?”

He answered very confidently.

“Mr Koh, last year sales RM5 million. So company value should be around RM5million lah.”

I smiled. This is where many SME bosses get valuation wrong.

Sales RM5million does not mean company value RM5 million.

A buyer does not pay you because your sales look big.
A buyer pays for profit.
A buyer pays for cash flow.
A buyer pays for systems.
A buyer pays for customers that can stay.
A buyer pays for a business that can still run after the boss walks out.

This is the painful part.

To the boss, the company is his baby.
30 years of hard work.
Sunday also work.
Public holiday also answer customer call.
Bank loan, supplier pressure, staff problem, customer problem, IRB letter, everything also he handles.

So when someone says the company may not be worth what he thinks, he feels hurt.

But valuation is not based on feeling.

A company with RM5 million sales but only 2% net margin may be less attractive than a smaller company with RM3 million sales and strong recurring profit.

Revenue is nice for storytelling.
Profit is nicer for valuation.
Cash flow is even nicer.
And clean documentation is the most beautiful.

Many SME bosses also think audited accounts already equal valuation.
No.
Audited accounts answer one question : “Are the financial statements fairly presented?”

Valuation asks another question : “What will a serious buyer actually pay for this business?”

Very different question.
Because a buyer will ask:

Are the profits sustainable?
Are customers too dependent on the founder?
Are personal expenses mixed inside the company?
Are directors’ salaries at market rate?
Are related party transactions properly recorded?
Can the business continue without the boss sitting in office every day?

If the answer is no, the value will be discounted.
Sometimes very heavily.

Now valuation is no longer only for selling business.
It matters for Capital Gains Tax on unlisted shares.
It matters for stamp duty on share transfers.
It matters for succession planning.
It matters when shareholders want to exit.
It matters when family business passes to the next generation.
It matters when IRB asks, “How did you arrive at this value?”

The biggest mistake?

Many SME owners only think about valuation when someone wants to buy their company.

By then, too late already.

Value is built years before the sale.
Clean accounts.
Less boss dependency.
Better margins.
Good systems.
Clear documents.
Proper governance.

All these boring things make buyers pay better.

So boss, don’t wait until someone offers you a low price, then only get angry and say : “Why my business so cheap?”

PS : Authored by Mr Koh Teck Peng, Chartered Accountant, Malaysia and Member of IACV (International Association of Certified Valuators).

KEEPING FINANCIAL RECORDS CAN IMPROVE YOUR CHANCES OF GETTING A LOAN

A business owner once walked into our office seeking a loan to expand her business. She was confident. Her shop was busy. Customers came in regularly. Sales appeared strong, and from her explanation, the business seemed profitable.

When the loan assessment process began, she was asked a simple question:

"Can you show us your sales records, expenses, and cash flow for the past few months?"

She paused. Her response was one I've heard many times:

"Everything is in my head."

The challenge was not that she lacked business experience. The challenge was that there was little documented evidence to support the figures she provided.

A few weeks later, another business owner applied for a similar facility. His business was smaller, but he arrived with a notebook containing daily sales records, expense tracking, inventory details, and account statements. The difference was clear.

One applicant relied on memory.

The other relied on records.

For lenders, records provide confidence. They help answer important questions:

✔️ How much does the business actually earn?

✔️ What are the regular expenses?

✔️ Is the cash flow sufficient to support loan repayment?

✔️ Is the business growing or struggling?

Without proper records, even a profitable business may find it difficult to demonstrate its true financial strength.

One of the most valuable habits any entrepreneur can develop is keeping accurate financial records. You don't need complicated accounting software to start.

A simple notebook, spreadsheet, or daily record book can make a significant difference.

Remember:

Good financial records don't just help you understand your business; they help others trust your business too. And in lending, trust is often the foundation of approval.

Do you currently keep records of your income and expenses, or do you rely mostly on memory?

(Tax Update) Boss, you think Tax Appeal is "Argue first, Talk reason"? 

Most of the time,
you pay first,
then slowly talk reason.

Uncle Chen walked into my office last month, face pale pale one.
Hand holding one LHDN assessment notice. Form JA.
Amount: RM380,000.

He sit down, straight away bang the table:
"I don't agree! I want to appeal!"

I looked at him, asked one question:
"Can. You want to appeal, no problem."
"But this RM380,000,
you know you may still need to pay first or not?"

He went quiet.
Just now the fire,
suddenly turned into cold sweat.

Because many SME bosses think,
tax dispute is like this:
I don't agree.
I appeal.
We sit down and talk.
Wait for the result, then only pay.
Reality is not like that one.

Under Malaysia tax system,
once the assessment notice Form JA is issued,
the tax usually must be paid within the period stated in the notice.
Appeal, doesn't mean automatic stop paying ah.

In English they call it :
Pay First, Appeal Later.

In Chinese, more straight:
先给钱, 再讲道理.

Sounds very harsh hor.
But this is the reality of Section 103 of the Income Tax Act.

The government's stand (past, present, and future) is very clear.

If everybody receive assessment then appeal,
then don't pay tax,
how is the country supposed to collect revenue?

So the rule is:
You can argue.
You can appeal.
You can talk reason.
But the money,
most of the time, you must arrange first.

This is where SME bosses suffer the most.
Not whether you have a case or not.

It's whether your cashflow can tahan,
until you finish talking your reason.

More realistic part is,
tax appeal is not today appeal,
tomorrow SCIT open court,
next month got result.
The cases are queuing,
maybe not a few months.
Maybe a few years.

Your money already paid.
Your case still queuing.
Your company still need to pay salary.
Suppliers still need to settle.
Bank loan still need to service.
Customers maybe still drag and drag.

At this point, tax dispute is not just a legal problem already.

It's a cashflow problem.
It's a "business live or die" problem.

Many bosses ask me:
"So I am very jialat lah?"

I usually say:
"Jialat or not, depends on whether you prepare ahead or not."

KTP gives SME bosses three simple reminders:

First, treat tax dispute as a cashflow event.
When the assessment notice come, don't only think:
"Who can help me argue?"

You also must immediately think:
"If really need to pay first, where this money coming from?"

Second, before the deadline, go and talk to LHDN.

Don't wait until last minute.

If the company really got cashflow problem,
you can try to apply for instalment or extension.

But you must take the first step.
You also must prepare proper financial documents,
show them you are not purposely dragging.

Third, your documents must be in order from day one.

I'm just the marketing guy here at Inflow Finance, and as I sit in the office and overhear client conversations, I can see the significant capacity we have to understand the nuances of every funding request. Three SMEs were declined refinancing last quarter — not because of current performance, but because of credit events from 2021.

When does a borrower's past stop defining their future?

The conversation around credit history in Nigeria often focuses on punishment for default. But what we rarely discuss at the policy level is the pathway back.

A credit bureau system that only records failure without providing structured rehabilitation does two things: it creates a permanent underclass of excluded enterprises, and it reduces the total pool of bankable businesses in an economy that desperately needs growth.

Here's what concerns me most.

The current system assumes that time alone heals credit wounds. But SMEs operating in our macroeconomic environment face shocks that are often systemic — forex volatility, input cost inflation, or supply chain disruptions that have nothing to do with management competence.

Yet their credit records treat all defaults as equal moral failures.

Progressive credit history frameworks in other markets include provisions for: graduated rehabilitation timelines based on debt clearance milestones, distinctions between economic-driven and willful defaults, and formal mechanisms for rebuilding creditworthiness through supervised lending windows.

We need these conversations at the regulatory table.

The Central Bank's guidelines on credit reporting are comprehensive on capture and retention. But they're almost silent on restoration and reintegration.

This isn't just about fairness. It's about economic efficiency.

Every viable business locked out of formal finance either migrates to predatory informal channels or shuts down entirely. Both outcomes shrink our tax base, reduce employment, and weaken the financial system's reach.

If we're serious about deepening financial inclusion and supporting Nigeria's real economy, we need credit systems that are designed for resilience, not just compliance.

To regulators and policy architects working on credit infrastructure reform: let's explore what graduated credit rehabilitation could look like in our context. My DMs are open for structured conversations.

Raksasa furnitur asal Swedia, IKEA, mengumumkan akan menutup 7 toko berukuran besar di China mulai Februari 2026. Langkah ini bukan penarikan total, melainkan penyesuaian strategi bisnis di tengah melemahnya daya beli masyarakat dan krisis sektor properti.

Toko-toko yang akan ditutup tersebar di kota-kota besar seperti Shanghai, Guangzhou, Tianjin, Nantong, Xuzhou, Ningbo, dan Harbin. Lesunya pasar properti membuat permintaan furnitur rumah tangga ikut turun, diperparah ketidakpastian ekonomi global dan perubahan perilaku belanja konsumen.

Sebagai gantinya, IKEA akan beralih ke format toko kecil dan kanal digital. Dalam dua tahun ke depan, mereka berencana membuka belasan toko berukuran kecil di Beijing dan Shenzhen, sekaligus memperkuat penjualan online lewat website, aplikasi, serta platform e-commerce seperti Tmall dan JD.com. Strategi ini juga untuk menghadapi persaingan ketat dari ritel lokal China yang menawarkan harga lebih murah dan pengiriman lebih cepat.

Menariknya, meski penjualan melemah, gerai IKEA di China tetap ramai pengunjung. Fenomena unik yang sudah berlangsung lebih dari satu dekade adalah kebiasaan warga tidur, rebahan, atau sekadar bersantai di display IKEA. Bagi banyak orang, IKEA bukan hanya tempat belanja, tapi ruang publik ber-AC gratis untuk istirahat dan mencoba produk langsung. Meski sempat dilarang, praktik ini masih terus berlangsung dan dianggap sebagai bagian dari budaya sosial.

Toko mungkin tutup, tapi cerita IKEA di China jelas belum selesai.

The hardest part of chasing a late payment isn't the first reminder. It's knowing how your tone should shift as the silence stretches on.

The rule: get clearer, not angrier.

Day 1-3 → Assume it got buried. Keep it light and short.
Day 7-10 → Add structure: invoice number, amount, due date, offer to help.
Day 14-21 → Make the clear ask. Name a date. Ask a direct question.
Day 30 → Set a firm, respectful boundary you actually intend to hold.

Three things never change: respect, clarity, and an easy path to pay. And never make a threat you won't keep.

A respectful boundary almost never costs you a client worth keeping. 💛

Accounts Payable ÷ (Cost of Goods Sold ÷ 365)

Example:

A business with $200,000 in accounts payable and $1.5M in annual COGS has a DPO of ~49 days.

Now here’s why it matters.

DPO is not just an accounting metric.

It is working capital strategy.

The longer you take to pay suppliers (within agreed terms), the more cash you retain in the business at any point in time.

In simple terms:

Higher DPO = suppliers are financing more of your operations.

But DPO only makes sense in context.

Working capital is a system:

DSO (how fast customers pay you)

* Inventory Days (how long cash sits in stock)
 – DPO (how long you take to pay suppliers)

That is your cash conversion cycle.

And it determines how much cash your business actually needs to operate.

Two simple comparisons:

A business collecting in 30 days and paying in 45 days is being financed by suppliers.

A business collecting in 60 days and paying in 30 days is financing everyone else.

Same revenue.

Completely different cash reality.

So how do you improve DPO without damaging supplier relationships?

1. Negotiate terms upfront

Don’t delay payments.

Design terms properly at the beginning of the relationship.

2. Pay predictably

Suppliers extend better terms to businesses that are reliable, not erratic.

3. Renegotiate as you scale

If you’ve grown from “small customer” to “meaningful volume,” revisit terms annually.

Most founders leave this untouched for years.

Which is why they unintentionally self-fund their supply chain.

Every additional day of DPO is retained working capital.

At scale, that becomes material cash.

Working capital is rarely a revenue problem.

It is usually a timing problem.

Most business owners have a leakage problem.

Your business can be profitable on paper and still be bleeding cash.

Leakage doesn't show up in one big line item. It shows up across five small places, every single month, until the damage is already done.

Here are the five most common cash leak points I see in growing businesses:

1. 𝐋𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 - Clients pay weeks after the due date. Every delayed payment is a loan you didn't agree to give.

2. 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 — Subscriptions auto-renewing for tools nobody uses. Do a monthly cost review. Cut what doesn't serve today.

3. 𝐌𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲 - Drawing from the business account without a system is not a salary. It's a slow drain.

4. 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 - Last-minute stock purchases at higher prices. Set reorder levels. Consolidate. Negotiate terms in advance.

5. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐭 - Tax shouldn't arrive as a crisis. Set aside a percentage every month into a dedicated tax account. Make it a fixed outflow, not a surprise.

Plugging is the precondition for building a business that actually works.

You cannot measure how well your cash is working if it is silently disappearing at the same time.

What is a cashflow forecast — and how often should you update it?

A cashflow forecast is simply a projection of the money coming in and going out of your business over a set period — usually the next 3 to 6 months.

It's not a guarantee. It's a map.

And like any map, it's only useful if it's up to date.

Here's what a basic cashflow forecast tracks:

→ Expected income (based on invoices raised or sales expected)
→ Known outgoings (rent, wages, subscriptions, supplier payments)
→ Timing — because when “money moves” matters as much as how much

The result? You can see, in advance, whether you're likely to hit a cash tight spot. That gives you options. Options you don't have if you're discovering the problem when it's already here.

How often should you update it?

Monthly as a minimum. Weekly if your cashflow is variable or your margins are tight.

It doesn't need to be complicated. A simple spreadsheet, kept current, can make a real difference.

What Business Owners Learn Too Late About Cash Flow

Most business owners focus on revenue first.

More sales.
More customers.
More growth.

And while those things matter, many founders eventually learn an important lesson:

Revenue attracts attention.

Cash flow determines survival.

Unfortunately, this lesson is often learned too late.

In the early stages, strong sales create confidence.

The business appears healthy.
Orders are increasing.
Opportunities are expanding.

But as operations grow, so do financial demands.

Inventory requires funding.
Suppliers need payment.
Salaries must be paid on time.
And expenses continue regardless of when customers pay.

This is where many businesses face an unexpected reality.

A company can look successful on paper while cash remains under pressure.

The problem is not always profitability.

It is timing.

Money may be earned today but received weeks or months later.

Meanwhile, obligations arrive right now.

Another lesson founders learn late is that cash-flow problems rarely appear suddenly.

They build gradually.

Through delayed collections.
Poor visibility.
Unplanned expansion.
And decisions made without understanding future liquidity needs.

That is why experienced business owners track cash flow as closely as they track sales.

They monitor collections.
Forecast obligations.
And create financial breathing room before pressure appears.

Because growth alone does not create stability.

Liquidity does.

And in the long run, the businesses that remain strongest are often not the ones with the highest revenue.

They are the ones that understand how cash moves through the business.

But over time, I noticed something: emailing and calling alone don’t automatically move cash.

What actually makes the difference is the strategy behind both:

• Knowing when an email is enough vs. when a call will actually create urgency.

• Having a consistent follow-up rhythm instead of reacting day by day.

• Tracking promises with clear next steps, not just logging notes.

• Knowing when to escalate instead of repeating the same message.

Escalation paths matter more than we admit. Without them, things just keep circling. With them, decisions finally start moving.

The biggest shift for me was moving from “Did I follow up?” to “Did I create movement?” Because in AR, being busy is easy. Getting cash to actually move is the real work.

The most dangerous inventory operation is not the one that is chaotic.

It is the one that feels organised while the same stockouts happen every quarter.

The team is working hard.

The warehouse looks structured.

The reports are being filed.

Yet the same problems keep returning.

Here is the myth hiding underneath it:

Myth: If the process looks structured, the rules must be working.

Truth: In many operations, inventory decisions are either undocumented or applied differently by each person responsible for them.

That inconsistency drives stockouts, overstock, and cash flow issues.

5 rules that help eliminate this pattern:

1️⃣ Define minimum and maximum stock levels at the SKU level

Category-level targets create false confidence.

Stockouts happen at the SKU level, so controls should too.

2️⃣ Standardise reorder point calculations

When buyers use different logic for the same decision, results become unpredictable.

Use one documented method and review it regularly.

3️⃣ Fix system trust issues directly

If teams manually verify inventory before purchasing, the problem is not process.

The problem is trust in the data.

Every decision built on unreliable information carries the same risk.

4️⃣ Create a clear escalation path for accuracy issues

Most inventory exceptions are handled reactively.

Define thresholds, assign ownership, and establish the response process before problems occur.

The most expensive decisions are often the ones made under pressure.

5️⃣ Measure inventory accuracy as a cash flow metric

Inventory accuracy is not just an operational KPI.

It directly impacts working capital.

When leaders connect accuracy to financial outcomes, purchasing discipline improves, forecasting becomes stronger, and accountability increases.

The operations that protect cash flow are not always the most sophisticated.

They are usually the most consistent.

If you reviewed your inventory rules today, how many are formally documented and how many exist only in the habits of your most experienced employees?
